title: The Generalization Spectrum: A Chromatographic Approach to Evaluating Learning Algorithms
claim: Ranking learning methods by transfer distance, rather than one aggregate score, reveals profile differences and rank swaps that single scores hide.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; level schematic plus table, then annotated line plot
description: Two rounded panels. Panel A, titled Generalization Spectrum, shows a rainbow gradient arrow labeled 'Increasing transfer distance'. Below it is a row of five colored circles, D0 to D4, each with an icon and a label: Exact Recall, Impl. Transfer, Context Transfer, Category Matched and Unpaired Baseline. Colored brackets group the levels as Memorization, Near Transfer and Far Transfer / In-domain Baseline. Under the brackets, a checkmark/cross table lists Format, Narrative, Exec. Spec. and Family against D0 to D4, showing which attributes are still shared at each level. Panel B is a line plot of pass@1 against evaluation level, with curves for Baseline, ICL, SFT and RL. Numbered callout bubbles mark matched memorization at D0, SFT dropping quickly, ICL being stable near but dropping far, and rankings swapping. A gradient arrow under the x-axis repeats the distance cue.
caption: The Generalization Spectrum. (A) To measure how far learning transfers from a training seed, we construct paired evaluation variants at increasing transfer distance. Each level removes one attribute shared with the seed: format (the surface code realization), narrative (the natural-language context, excluding the formal I/O contract), executable specification (the I/O contract, solution logic, and tests), and family (the algorithmic category). Thus D0 shares all four (exact recall); D1 drops format (implementation transfer); D2 additionally drops narrative (context transfer); D3 retains only family (category-matched); and D4 shares none (unpaired in-domain baseline). (B) Plotting pass@1 against transfer distance yields a Generalization Profile. At matched memorization (D0), GRPO yields stronger near-transfer than SFT—especially on implementation (D1) and context (D2) transfer—while paired ICL stays strong through the instance-paired levels (D0–D2) and then drops at the category-matched and unpaired levels (D3–D4), exposing a correspondence bottleneck rather than uniformly stable transfer. Method rankings swap with distance, a distinction invisible to any single aggregate score.
abstract: Traditional evaluations measure a learning algorithm's final performance on an i.i.d. test set, reducing learning to a single aggregate score. This approach obscures a fundamental question: to what extent does learning from a specific example generalize to others? Such per-sample generalization, akin to learning by analogy in human cognition, captures how far the knowledge extracted from one example can transfer, yet remains invisible to standard benchmarks. We introduce the Generalization Spectrum, an evaluation framework designed to expose this hidden dimension. For each training example, we construct a controlled suite of test variants arranged by increasing transfer distance, from exact recall to implementation transfer across languages, context transfer under complete narrative re-framing, category-matched in-domain problems, and an unpaired baseline. By tracking performance across these distances, we reveal not just whether an algorithm learns, but how far that learning extends. We instantiate this framework on competitive programming, using a selection-and-synthesis pipeline seeded with recent problems to mitigate contamination. We first compare three canonical learning paradigms under matched memorization. RL converts memorization into near-transfer more efficiently than SFT-family baselines, while ICL exhibits strong but correspondence-dependent transfer. We then use the Spectrum to diagnose within-family variants. The resulting profiles show that local gains need not expand the generalization radius: abstractions and hints mainly lift local transfer, RFT preserves a stronger far-transfer tail than reference SFT, and self-distillation or hint-assisted RL can reduce far transfer even when local transfer or optimization improves.
